questions: Did your walking problem begin suddenly, over hours or days?
Has it been getting progressively worse?
Have you had any falls or near-falls because of this problem?
Do you feel the room spinning or feel unusually lightheaded when walking?
Do you have weakness on one side of your body?
Do you have numbness or loss of sensation in your feet or legs?
Do you have pain in your hips, knees, back, or feet that limits your walking?
Do you have difficulty seeing where you are stepping, even with your glasses or contacts?
Do you feel unsteady even when sitting or lying down?
Does your walking improve when you are distracted or not thinking about it?
Can you walk normally when alone but have more difficulty when someone is watching?
Can you walk backward more easily than you can walk forward?
Can you walk normally on stairs or on uneven ground?
Have you had any recent head injury, stroke-like episode, infection, or hospitalization?
Do you have a history of seizures, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease, or another neurologic disorder?
Have you recently started or increased any medication, alcohol, or sedative that could affect your balance?
Do you have new problems controlling your bladder or bowels?
Do you have double vision, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, or severe headache?
Have you been under unusual emotional stress before this walking problem began?
Do you believe you may fall even when you are physically able to take the step?

results: 1. Comprehensive bedside neurologic examination with functional gait assessment, including forward/backward walking, tandem gait, toe and heel walking, Romberg testing, dual-task gait, and Hoover sign
Romberg test: negative - swaying is not worse with the eyes closed
deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses: normal
coordination examination (limb and truncal): limb and truncal ataxia
2. MRI of the brain with and without gadolinium contrast
brain MRI: cerebellar atrophy on sagittal T1 and axial FLAIR
MRI brain with gadolinium: cerebellar atrophy without gadolinium enhancement
3. Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, thyroid-stimulating hormone, vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, folate, copper, and hemoglobin A1c
vitamin B12 with methylmalonic acid: normal
copper / caeruloplasmin: normal - excludes Wilson disease
serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine: normal
4. Formal speech, swallowing, and ocular-motor examination by neurology
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Sporadic adult-onset degenerative cerebellar ataxia (idiopathic late-onset cerebellar ataxia) with cerebellar atrophy

ALTERNATIVE 1: Genetic spinocerebellar ataxia, particularly spinocerebellar ataxia type 6

ALTERNATIVE 2: Multiple-system atrophy, cerebellar type

ALTERNATIVE 3: Immune-mediated cerebellar ataxia, including gluten-sensitive or paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration
